title: Tensor analysis in special relativity
one_line_summary: Rebuilds the Minkowski dot product as a bilinear machine and from that single idea develops one-forms (pictured as stacks of surfaces), the gradient, outer products, symmetry, the metric's role in turning vectors into one-forms, general (M N) tensors, index gymnastics and the derivative of a tensor field in flat spacetime.
role_in_book: Chapter 2 gave four-vectors and the scalar product; Chapter 4 needs the stress-energy tensor and Chapters 5-6 need tensors in curvilinear coordinates and on manifolds. This chapter is the algebraic bridge: it installs the coordinate-free 'tensor = multilinear map' definition, the vector/one-form duality, and the metric as the extra structure that links them, all in the easy setting of Lorentz frames where basis vectors are the same everywhere. Its final remark (that differentiating components suffices only because the basis is constant) is deliberately planted as the doorway to the covariant derivative and hence to general relativity.

assumed_background.topic: Four-vectors, basis vectors of a Lorentz frame, component notation with the arrow-under-O convention
Einstein summation convention and dummy indices
Lorentz transformation matrix Lambda and its inverse, transformation of basis vectors versus components
Scalar product of four-vectors, e_alpha . e_beta = eta_alpha beta (Eq. 2.27), magnitudes and timelike/spacelike/null classification (Eq. 2.24), linearity of the dot product (Exercise 2.34)
Four-velocity as the tangent to a world line parametrized by proper time
Abstract vector spaces, linear independence, bases, matrix multiplication, inverse and transpose, determinants
Multivariable chain rule and partial derivatives
Gradient, level surfaces and normal vectors in Euclidean vector calculus
Hilbert space of wave functions, complex inner product, Dirac bra-ket notation (only for an optional analogy)
Notion of a group (for the Lorentz-group exercises)

learning_objectives: State the definition of a (0 N) tensor as a real-valued map of N vectors that is linear in each slot, and verify that the dot product g(A,B) meets it.
Compute the components of any tensor by feeding it basis vectors (and basis one-forms), and reconstruct its value on arbitrary arguments from those components.

Explain why one-form components transform with Lambda^beta_alpha-bar (like basis vectors) while vector components use the inverse matrix, and prove that the contraction A^alpha p_alpha is frame independent.
Construct the dual basis from a vector basis e_alpha via omega-tilde^alpha(e_beta) = delta^alpha_beta, and explain why changing one basis vector can change all four dual basis one-forms.
Draw a one-form as a stack of parallel surfaces and evaluate it on a vector by counting surfaces crossed, including for the gradient on a contour map.

Derive from the chain rule along a world line that the partial derivatives of a scalar field are the components of a one-form d-tilde phi, and check its transformation law via dx^beta/dx^alpha-bar = Lambda^beta_alpha-bar.
Use the comma notation phi_{,alpha}, and identify the basis one-forms with the coordinate gradients d-tilde x^alpha.
Define a normal one-form and an outward normal one-form without using the metric, and explain the odd behaviour of outward normal vectors on surfaces of different causal type.

Form outer products of one-forms, show that omega-tilde^alpha tensor omega-tilde^beta is a basis for (0 2) tensors, and split any (0 2) tensor uniquely into symmetric and antisymmetric parts with the () and [] notation.

Use the metric to map a vector to a one-form (V_alpha = eta_alpha beta V^beta) and the inverse metric to map back, recognising that in Minkowski components this just flips the sign of the time component.
Compute magnitudes and inner products of one-forms with eta^alpha beta and classify one-forms as timelike, spacelike or null.
Treat vectors as linear functions of one-forms, define (M N) tensors, write their component transformation law, and raise or lower any index with the metric.
Show that the mixed components of the metric are the Kronecker delta and articulate why the metric is extra structure (Riemannian vs pseudo-Riemannian, non-metric spaces).
Differentiate a tensor field along a world line, identify the gradient nabla T as a tensor with one extra covariant slot, and state which assumption (constant basis) will fail in curved spacetime.

teaching_approach.summary: A patient, geometry-first build-up that starts from something the reader already owns (the Minkowski dot product) and reinterprets it as a function of vectors, then climbs one rank at a time: (0 1), (0 2), metric map, (M N), derivative. Every new object is defined by what it does to arguments, components are derived as values on basis elements, and transformation laws are obtained rather than postulated. Pictures (sheets pierced by arrows, contour maps) carry the intuition for one-forms, and the minus sign in eta is used as the reason the vector/one-form distinction cannot be ignored in relativity. Frequent 'why distinguish?', 'circular reasoning?' and 'why the metric?' interludes anticipate learner objections.
narrative_arc: Rewrite the familiar scalar product as a double sum A^alpha B^beta eta_alpha beta and notice it is a rule turning two vectors into a number.
Promote that observation to the definition of a (0 N) tensor as a multilinear real-valued function; name the metric g and define components as values on basis vectors.
Specialise to (0 1) tensors: one-forms form a vector space (the dual space); derive their component transformation and prove contraction is invariant.
Build the dual basis from the vector basis, stress that components alone mean nothing without a basis, and give the transformation of basis one-forms.
Offer a metric-free picture of a one-form as stacked surfaces; justify it with the gradient of a scalar field sampled along a world line and with a contour map.
Check the gradient's transformation law, introduce comma derivatives, identify basis one-forms with coordinate gradients, and define normal one-forms.
Climb to (0 2) tensors: outer products, a 16-element basis, symmetric and antisymmetric parts; note that g is symmetric.

Let the metric with one empty slot turn a vector into a one-form; find the sign-flip rule, the inverse metric, the vector gradient, and explain via Euclidean space why elementary courses never needed the distinction.
Draw the duality out with row/column vectors and bra-kets, then define magnitudes and inner products of one-forms and unit normals, flagging peculiar outward normals.
Complete the duality by letting vectors eat one-forms, define (M N) tensors and their transformation, and defuse the 'circular definition' worry.
Generalise the metric map to index raising and lowering on any tensor, show eta^alpha_beta = delta, and discuss why the metric (rather than some other tensor) is the chosen extra structure.

Differentiate a (1 1) tensor field along a world line, extract the (1 2) gradient nabla T and the directional derivative nabla_U T, and point out that constant basis vectors are the hidden assumption that GR will remove.
signature_moves: Definitions are phrased as 'feed the machine arguments'; components are always obtained by feeding basis elements, so every component formula is derived in two lines from linearity.
Slot notation with blanks, g(V, _ ), used to manufacture new tensors by partially filling arguments (metric map in §3.6, fixing U in nabla T in §3.9).
Transformation laws are presented as the 'only equation one can write with indices in the right places', teaching index placement as a consistency check.
Surfaces-pierced-by-arrow picture of a one-form, justified physically through the gradient and a hiking contour map with explicit contour counts (1.5, 2, 0.5).
Uses the lone minus sign in eta as the pedagogical lever: in Euclidean Cartesian coordinates vectors and one-forms have identical components, so the distinction only becomes visible in SR.
Anticipatory 'objection' interludes (Why distinguish one-forms from vectors? Circular reasoning? Metric and nonmetric vector algebras) that voice and answer the reader's doubts.
Draws on other parts of physics (matrix row/column vectors, Hilbert space with complex conjugation acting as the metric, Dirac bras and kets, phase space, spinor space) to show duality is ubiquitous.
Ends the chapter by exposing the one simplifying assumption (constant basis) that will break, turning a technical remark into the motivation for the next part of the book.

sections.title: The metric tensor
sections.summary: Expands two vectors on a frame basis and uses linearity of the dot product to write it as A^alpha B^beta eta_alpha beta. The numbers eta_alpha beta are thereby recast as the recipe that turns a pair of vectors into a single number, previewing the idea that such a recipe is what a tensor is.
key_moves: Use distinct dummy indices for the two expansions so the double sum is unambiguous.
Pull the basis dot products out by linearity and recognise them as eta_alpha beta (Eq. 2.27).
Read the result as a frame-invariant form of -A^0B^0 + A^1B^1 + A^2B^2 + A^3B^3 and as a rule mapping two vectors to a number.

sections.title: Definition of tensors
sections.summary: Defines a (0 N) tensor as a real-valued function of N vectors that is linear in each argument, and checks that the dot product is a (0 2) tensor, named g. Emphasises that the definition refers to vectors, not their components, so a tensor gives frame-independent numbers; a scalar function is a (0 0) tensor. An aside separates a function f from its value f(x). Components in a frame are defined as the values on basis vectors, giving g(e_alpha, e_beta) = eta_alpha beta.
concepts: function versus value of a function
key_moves: State linearity in each argument separately (Eq. 3.2) and combine into g(aA + bB, C) = a g(A,C) + b g(B,C).
Stress that the tensor acts on the vectors themselves; frame dependence enters only when components are taken.
Define components as the tensor evaluated on basis vectors, so eta_alpha beta is the component array of g in a Lorentz frame.

sections.title: The (0 1) tensors: one-forms
sections.summary: One-forms (covectors, dual vectors) are linear maps from vectors to numbers; with pointwise addition and scaling they form the dual vector space. Components p_alpha = p(e_alpha) give p(A) = A^alpha p_alpha, a contraction needing no metric. One-form components transform with the same matrix as basis vectors and hence inversely to vector components, which is proved to keep the contraction invariant; the old co/contra names are explained and retired. The dual basis omega-tilde^alpha is defined by omega-tilde^alpha(e_beta) = delta^alpha_beta, relates whole bases rather than pairs, and transforms like vector components. The section closes with the picture of a one-form as a family of surfaces whose value on a vector is the number of surfaces pierced.
concepts: picture of a one-form as stacked surfaces
key_moves: Derive p(A) = A^alpha p_alpha from linearity (Eq. 3.8) and emphasise all plus signs: no metric involved.
Evaluate p on the new basis e_beta-bar = Lambda^alpha_beta-bar e_alpha to get p_beta-bar = Lambda^alpha_beta-bar p_alpha (Eq. 3.9).
Show Lambda^mu_alpha-bar Lambda^alpha-bar_beta = delta^mu_beta makes A^alpha-bar p_alpha-bar = A^beta p_beta (Eqs. 3.10a-d).
Require p = p_alpha omega-tilde^alpha to reproduce Eq. 3.8 for all A, forcing omega-tilde^alpha(e_beta) = delta^alpha_beta (Eq. 3.12).
Warn that a quadruple of numbers is meaningless without saying which basis (and which kind of basis) it refers to.
Argue that a picture of a one-form must not depend on a metric, which rules out an arrow and leads to the sliced-space picture.

sections.title: Gradient of a function is a one-form
sections.summary: A scalar field sampled along a world line changes at a rate d phi/d tau that the chain rule writes as a linear function of the four-velocity; hence the partial derivatives are the components of a one-form, the gradient d-tilde phi. A topographic map shows why: elevation gained along a displacement equals the number of contours crossed. The sliced-space picture is refined to straight parallel surfaces at a point, and it is argued that turning the gradient into an arrow needs a notion of length, i.e. a metric. The gradient's components transform correctly because dx^beta/dx^alpha-bar = Lambda^beta_alpha-bar. Comma notation is introduced, basis one-forms are identified with d-tilde x^alpha, d-tilde f is warned not to be an infinitesimal, and normal and outward normal one-forms are defined without a metric.
concepts: directional derivative of a scalar along a world line
picture of a one-form as stacked surfaces
key_moves: Parametrise a world line by proper time and apply the chain rule to phi(t(tau), x(tau), ...) (Eq. 3.14).
Recognise d phi/d tau as linear in U, so the partials are one-form components (Eq. 3.15).
Count contours on a map: displacement 1 gains 1.5 contours, 2 gains 2, 3 only 0.5, illustrating Delta h = (dh)(Delta x).
Explain that 'steepest direction' requires 'per unit length', hence a metric, before a gradient vector exists.

Compare the required one-form transformation (Eq. 3.16) with the chain-rule transformation (Eq. 3.17); they agree because x^beta = Lambda^beta_alpha-bar x^alpha-bar with constant coefficients (Eq. 3.18).
Note x^alpha_{,beta} = delta^alpha_beta and compare with Eq. 3.12 to conclude that omega-tilde^alpha is d-tilde x^alpha (Eq. 3.20).

sections.title: The (0 2) tensors
sections.summary: The outer product p tensor q is the simplest (0 2) tensor, and it is not commutative. A general (0 2) tensor has 16 components f_alpha beta = f(e_alpha, e_beta); demanding f = f_alpha beta omega-tilde^alpha beta forces the basis to be omega-tilde^alpha tensor omega-tilde^beta, so every such tensor is a sum of outer products. Symmetric and antisymmetric tensors are defined through argument exchange, symmetrisation and antisymmetrisation are introduced with (alpha beta) and [alpha beta] index brackets, and any (0 2) tensor splits uniquely into the two parts. The metric is symmetric.
key_moves: Define (p tensor q)(A,B) = p(A) q(B) and contrast with (q tensor p)(A,B).
Expand f(A,B) = A^alpha B^beta f_alpha beta by bilinearity (Eq. 3.22).
Evaluate the proposed expansion on (e_mu, e_nu) to get omega-tilde^alpha beta(e_mu, e_nu) = delta^alpha_mu delta^beta_nu, recognised as a product of dual-basis values (Eqs. 3.24-3.25).
Define symmetry by argument exchange for all vectors, then specialise to basis vectors to get component symmetry.
Add and subtract halves to write h_alpha beta = h_(alpha beta) + h_[alpha beta] (Eq. 3.35).

sections.title: Metric as a mapping of vectors into one-forms
sections.summary: Feeding g a single vector leaves one empty slot, so g(V, _ ) is a one-form V-tilde with components V_alpha = eta_alpha beta V^beta: in a Lorentz frame the time component flips sign. Because eta has nonzero determinant an inverse eta^alpha beta exists, numerically equal to eta, making the vector/one-form map invertible and producing the vector gradient, which is orthogonal to level surfaces. Euclidean Cartesian coordinates hide the distinction because the metric is the identity. Dual spaces are illustrated by row and column vectors and by wave functions, where complex conjugation plays the metric's role (bras and kets). Magnitudes and inner products of one-forms are defined through their associated vectors and computed with eta^alpha beta; normal vectors, unit normals and the causal type of three-surfaces are defined, with surprising directions for outward normal vectors.
concepts: metric as a map from vectors to one-forms
key_moves: Partially fill g to define V-tilde(A) = g(V, A) = V . A (Eqs. 3.37-3.38).
Compute V_alpha = V-tilde(e_alpha) = eta_alpha beta V^beta and read off V_0 = -V^0, V_i = V^i (Eqs. 3.39-3.42).
Invoke det(eta) = -1 to guarantee an inverse and define A^alpha = eta^alpha beta A_beta (Eq. 3.43).
Show the vector associated with d-tilde phi is orthogonal to vectors tangent to constant-phi surfaces because its dot product equals the rate of change of phi.
Contrast gradient components (Eq. 3.15) with vector-gradient components (Eq. 3.45) differing by the time-component sign.
Collapse eta_alpha beta eta^beta nu = delta_alpha^nu to write the one-form magnitude with the inverse metric alone (Eqs. 3.48-3.51).
Define the inner product of one-forms by polarisation (Eq. 3.52).

sections.title: Finally: (M N) tensors
sections.summary: Completes the duality: a vector is a linear function of one-forms, V(p) = p(V) = <p, V>, so vectors themselves are (1 0) tensors. An (M 0) tensor eats M one-forms, and an (M N) tensor eats M one-forms and N vectors; its components carry M upper and N lower indices, and each index transforms with its own Lambda placed as index positions dictate. A 'circular reasoning?' interlude explains that mathematics is indifferent to which space is taken as primary; physics enters by identifying displacements (or gradients) with one of them.
concepts: vectors as linear functions of one-forms
key_moves: Define V(p) := p(V) and introduce the symmetric pairing notation <p, V> (Eq. 3.54).
Build V tensor W with components V^alpha W^beta and basis e_alpha tensor e_beta.
Define R(omega-tilde^alpha; e_beta) = R^alpha_beta for a (1 1) tensor and transform it by substituting transformed basis elements (Eq. 3.55).
Answer the circularity worry: vectors and one-forms are mutually defined but the algebra is consistent; physical meaning is imported by modelling choices.

sections.title: Index 'raising' and 'lowering'
sections.summary: The metric and its inverse convert any tensor slot between vector-type and one-form-type, changing the tensor's type by moving one index down or up; the resulting tensors share a name and differ only by index position, and lowering different indices gives inequivalent tensors. In SR the rule is to flip the sign whenever a 0 index moves. Raising one index of eta gives the Kronecker delta, and raising both gives eta^alpha beta, so the metric's upper components are the matrix inverse of its lower ones. A closing discussion explains why a correspondence is needed only when scalar products matter (phase space manages without one), that the metric is added structure, distinguishes Riemannian from pseudo-Riemannian (and antisymmetric spinor) metrics, and notes that choosing other metric components leads to other spaces such as curved GR spacetime.
key_moves: Lower the second or the first upper index of T^alpha beta_gamma, or raise its lower index, to produce two inequivalent (1 2) tensors and a (3 0) tensor (Eqs. 3.56-3.58).
State the SR sign rule for time versus space indices.
Compute eta^alpha_beta = eta^alpha mu eta_mu beta = delta^alpha_beta as a matrix product of mutual inverses (Eqs. 3.59-3.60).
Separate the question 'why any correspondence?' (needed for scalar products) from 'why the metric?' (whatever tensor does the job is called the metric).

sections.title: Differentiation of tensors
sections.summary: Differentiating a tensor field raises its covariant rank by one, as with a function and its gradient. For a (1 1) field T expanded on a Lorentz basis, the derivative along a world line only hits the components because the basis one-forms and vectors are position independent; the chain rule then gives T^alpha_{beta,gamma} U^gamma. Since dT/d tau is a tensor for every U, the array T^alpha_{beta,gamma} defines a (1 2) tensor nabla T, and filling its derivative slot with U gives nabla_U T = dT/d tau. The chapter flags that constant basis vectors fail in curved spacetime, which is where GR begins.
concepts: directional derivative of a tensor along a vector
constant basis in a Lorentz frame
key_moves: Expand T = T^alpha_beta omega-tilde^beta tensor e_alpha and define dT/d tau as a limit of differences of tensors (Eqs. 3.61-3.62).
Use constancy of the basis to move the derivative onto the components (Eq. 3.63).
Apply the chain rule to get T^alpha_{beta,gamma} U^gamma (Eq. 3.64).
Argue that because the result is a tensor for arbitrary U, stripping U off leaves a (1 2) tensor nabla T (Eqs. 3.65-3.66).
Introduce nabla_U T for the derivative along U and flag that the constant-basis step will need replacing in GR (Eqs. 3.67-3.68).

sections.title: Bibliography
sections.summary: Points readers who want more of the geometric view of tensors to the early chapters of Misner, Thorne and Wheeler, to Schutz's Geometrical Methods of Mathematical Physics and to Bishop and Goldberg, and notes that most physics texts outside relativity only treat Cartesian tensors, citing Bourne and Kendall.
key_moves: Positions the chapter's approach (geometry of tensors over transformation rules) relative to standard references.

sections.title: Exercises
sections.summary: Thirty-four problems moving from index hygiene and numerical evaluation of one-forms, through dual bases, gradients from isotherm maps, normals on the t-x plane, outer products and symmetry, raising and lowering, and differentiation of explicit tensor fields, to projection tensors, the metric-preserving definition of Lorentz transformations, the Lorentz group, and a null basis built from u = t - x and v = t + x.
key_moves: Exercises 3.32-3.33 redefine Lorentz transformations as exactly those matrices preserving eta (Eq. 3.71), turning the metric into the defining structure of SR.
Exercise 3.31 builds the projection tensor orthogonal to a four-velocity, a tool used heavily for fluids later.
Exercise 3.34 shows a basis can consist of non-orthogonal null vectors, so metric components need not be diagonal.

concepts.name: metric tensor
aliases: eta_alpha beta as components of g
concepts.definition: The symmetric (0 2) tensor g whose value on two vectors is their scalar product; in any Lorentz frame its components g(e_alpha, e_beta) are eta_alpha beta = diag(-1, 1, 1, 1).
concepts.how_introduced: Reached by rewriting the chapter-2 dot product as the double sum A^alpha B^beta eta_alpha beta and noticing it is a rule producing a number from two vectors; named g once the tensor definition is in place, and later shown to be symmetric and to double as the vector-to-one-form converter.
concepts.notes: The book says the name will be 'justified later'; the justification is the tensor definition of §3.2 and the mapping role of §3.6.

concepts.name: tensor of type (0 N)
concepts.definition: A real-valued function of N vector arguments that is linear in each argument separately; its value does not depend on any frame, only its components do.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated immediately after observing that eta_alpha beta encodes a two-vector-to-number rule; the dot product is checked against the definition, and a scalar function is noted as the N = 0 case.
concepts.notes: The (0 N) label is used before it is explained; the upper/lower numbers are justified only in §3.7.

concepts.name: multilinearity
concepts.definition: The property that a function of several vector arguments is linear in every argument when the others are held fixed: scaling one argument scales the value, and additive splitting of one argument splits the value.
concepts.how_introduced: Spelled out for the dot product (Eq. 3.2 for the first slot and its partner for the second) and summarised in g(aA + bB, C) = a g(A,C) + b g(B,C); the reader is told to study it carefully because every later component formula comes from it.
formulas: \mathbf g(\alpha\vec A+\beta\vec B,\vec C)=\alpha\,\mathbf g(\vec A,\vec C)+\beta\,\mathbf g(\vec B,\vec C)

concepts.name: components of a tensor
concepts.definition: The frame-dependent numbers obtained by evaluating a tensor on the basis vectors (and, for upper indices, basis one-forms) of a chosen frame; together with the basis they reconstruct the tensor.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced right after the aside on functions, applied first to g to recover eta_alpha beta, then reused as the uniform recipe for one-forms (Eq. 3.7), (0 2) tensors (Eq. 3.21) and (M N) tensors.

concepts.name: scalar field as a (0 0) tensor
concepts.definition: A real-valued function of position such as f(t, x, y, z), classified as a tensor that takes no vector arguments at all.
concepts.how_introduced: A one-line remark after the tensor definition; later used as the starting rung for differentiation (the gradient of a (0 0) tensor is a (0 1) tensor).

concepts.name: function versus value of a function
concepts.definition: A function is the rule (mapping) f assigning outputs to inputs; f(x) is the particular output for input x. In tensor language g is the machine, while g(A,B) is a specific number.
concepts.how_introduced: A labelled aside in §3.2 takes apart y = f(x): the rule f is the function and f(x) is merely its output. It notes that school algebra lets x stand both for one particular number and for an arbitrary input. The aside prepares the reader to write g( , ) for the machine and g(A,B) for a number.

concepts.name: one-form
concepts.definition: A linear map from vectors to real numbers; the set of all such maps is itself a vector space, the dual of the space of vectors.
concepts.how_introduced: Treated as the simplest (0 N) tensor, denoted with a tilde; its vector-space structure is defined pointwise (Eqs. 3.6a-b), its components and transformation are derived, and it is then given a metric-free geometric picture and physically anchored by the gradient.
formulas: (\tilde p+\tilde q)(\vec A)=\tilde p(\vec A)+\tilde q(\vec A)
concepts.notes: The book notes that the names covector, covariant vector and one-form are often used interchangeably, and prefers one-form or dual vector.

concepts.name: dual vector space
concepts.definition: The vector space of all linear real-valued functions on a given vector space; it has the same dimension, and each basis of the original space induces a dual basis.
concepts.how_introduced: Named once one-forms are shown to add and scale like vectors; the word 'dual' is tied to the inverse transformation of components; later illustrated by row versus column vectors and by bras versus kets.
concepts.notes: The book also defines linear independence of one-forms (no nontrivial combination gives the zero one-form, which is zero on every vector), so any four independent one-forms could serve as a basis before the dual basis is singled out.

concepts.name: contraction
aliases: contraction of a one-form with a vector
concepts.definition: The metric-free number obtained by applying a one-form to a vector, p(V) = p_alpha V^alpha = sum with all plus signs; more generally, summing an upper index against a lower index.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived by linearity from the component expansion of the vector (Eq. 3.8), contrasted with the scalar product of two vectors that needs a third object, and later written symmetrically as <p, V> when vectors are recast as functions of one-forms.
formulas: \vec V(\tilde p):=\tilde p(\vec V)=p_\alpha V^\alpha:=\langle\tilde p,\vec V\rangle
concepts.notes: The book calls contraction more fundamental than the scalar product because it needs no additional tensor.

concepts.name: transformation law of one-form components
concepts.definition: Under a change of Lorentz frame the components of a one-form transform with Lambda^alpha_beta-bar, the same matrix that expresses new basis vectors in terms of old ones and the inverse of the matrix used for vector components.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by evaluating the one-form on the new basis vectors and using linearity (Eq. 3.9); the inverse relationship is then shown to guarantee invariance of the contraction (Eqs. 3.10a-d); confirmed independently for the gradient via the chain rule (Eqs. 3.16-3.18).

concepts.name: covariant and contravariant terminology
concepts.definition: Older names: indices or objects whose components transform like basis vectors are 'covariant' (lower indices, one-forms); those transforming oppositely are 'contravariant' (upper indices, vectors). An (M N) tensor is M-times contravariant and N-times covariant.
concepts.how_introduced: Explained etymologically after the proof of contraction invariance and partly retired as old-fashioned because it conflates a change of basis (new vectors from old) with a change of components (same object, new description); revived in §3.7 for index language.

concepts.name: dual basis
concepts.definition: Given a basis e_beta of vectors, the four one-forms omega-tilde^alpha fixed by omega-tilde^alpha(e_beta) = delta^alpha_beta; in this basis any one-form expands as p = p_alpha omega-tilde^alpha with p_alpha = p(e_alpha).
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by wanting a one-form basis in which the already-defined components p(e_alpha) are the expansion coefficients; the defining condition is forced by requiring p(A) = p_alpha A^alpha for all A. Components of the dual basis are written out, and the transformation law omega-tilde^alpha-bar = Lambda^alpha-bar_beta omega-tilde^beta is stated as the only index-consistent possibility.
concepts.notes: Two emphasised points: the duality relates the whole bases (changing e_0 alone generally alters all four omega-tilde^alpha), and a list of four numbers is meaningless without specifying the basis and whether it is a vector or one-form basis.

concepts.name: Kronecker delta
concepts.definition: The array equal to 1 when its two indices coincide and 0 otherwise; with one index up and one down it is the component array of the identity map and of the mixed metric.
concepts.how_introduced: Used first when multiplying Lambda by its inverse in the contraction proof, then as the defining value of basis one-forms on basis vectors, as x^alpha_{,beta}, and finally identified with the mixed components of the metric.

concepts.name: picture of a one-form as stacked surfaces
concepts.definition: Geometric representation of a one-form at a point as a family of equally spaced parallel surfaces (three-dimensional in spacetime); its value on a vector is the number of surfaces the arrow crosses, so closer spacing means a larger one-form.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by the need for a picture that does not presuppose a metric (an arrow cannot eat another arrow without one); introduced with Figure 3.1, justified through the gradient and contour maps (Figures 3.3 and 3.4), and refined to straight parallel surfaces because one-forms live at a point like tangent vectors.
concepts.notes: The picture shows orientation and relative size but cannot show a metric magnitude or causal type; a null one-form still has finitely spaced surfaces.

concepts.name: gradient one-form
aliases: exterior derivative of a function (modern name)
concepts.definition: For a scalar field phi, the one-form d-tilde phi whose value on a vector V is the rate of change of phi along V; in a Lorentz frame its components are the partial derivatives (phi_{,t}, phi_{,x}, phi_{,y}, phi_{,z}).
concepts.how_introduced: Derived by following a world line through a scalar field, applying the chain rule to get d phi/d tau as a linear function of the four-velocity (Eq. 3.14), and reading off one-form components (Eq. 3.15); then visualised with a topographic map and checked against the one-form transformation law, earning the label 'archetypal one-form'.
formulas: \tilde d\phi\to_{\mathcal O}(\partial\phi/\partial t,\partial\phi/\partial x,\partial\phi/\partial y,\partial\phi/\partial z)
concepts.notes: The book argues the elementary 'gradient vector' only exists once a metric supplies 'per unit length'.

concepts.name: directional derivative of a scalar along a world line
aliases: rate of change along a curve
concepts.definition: The derivative of a scalar field with respect to a curve's parameter, equal to the gradient one-form evaluated on the curve's tangent vector.
concepts.how_introduced: The motivating computation of §3.4 (Figure 3.2), later generalised to tensors in §3.9 where it becomes nabla_U T.

concepts.name: four-velocity
concepts.definition: The tangent vector to a world line parametrized by proper time, with components dx^alpha/d tau.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from chapter 2 as the vector on which the gradient acts to give the rate of change of a field seen by a moving observer; reused for the derivative of tensors.

concepts.name: comma notation for partial derivatives
concepts.definition: Shorthand phi_{,alpha} := partial phi / partial x^alpha; the index sits low because the coordinate index appears in the denominator and the object transforms as a one-form component.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced after verifying the gradient's transformation law; used immediately for x^alpha_{,beta} = delta^alpha_beta and later for tensor components T^alpha_{beta,gamma}. A footnote mentions the partial_alpha notation, which the book will not use.

concepts.name: coordinate basis one-forms dx^alpha
concepts.definition: The dual basis one-forms of a Lorentz frame are exactly the gradients of the coordinate functions, omega-tilde^alpha = d-tilde x^alpha, so any gradient expands as d-tilde f = f_{,alpha} d-tilde x^alpha.
concepts.how_introduced: Deduced by comparing x^alpha_{,beta} = delta^alpha_beta with the dual-basis condition (Eq. 3.12); followed by a caution that the resulting formula only resembles the physicist's infinitesimal differential.
concepts.notes: The book writes Eq. 3.20 with ':=' although it is a derived identity.

concepts.name: normal one-form
concepts.definition: A one-form that vanishes on every vector tangent to a given surface; if the surface bounds a region, it is an outward normal one-form when it is positive on vectors pointing out of the region. No metric is required.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as the natural replacement for a normal vector, which needs a scalar product to define orthogonality; the gradient of f is asserted (Exercise 3.13) to be normal to constant-f surfaces.
concepts.notes: Exercise 3.12 establishes uniqueness up to scale and consistency of sign on each side of a surface.

concepts.name: outer product
concepts.definition: For one-forms p and q, the (0 2) tensor p tensor q whose value on (A, B) is p(A) q(B); generalises to any tensors by multiplying values with arguments distributed in order. It is not commutative.
concepts.how_introduced: Offered as the simplest (0 2) tensor at the start of §3.5, with non-commutativity illustrated by swapping the argument roles; used to build bases for all tensor types.
formulas: (\tilde p\otimes\tilde q)(\vec A,\vec B)=\tilde p(\vec A)\,\tilde q(\vec B)

concepts.name: basis for (0 2) tensors
concepts.definition: The 16 outer products of dual basis one-forms form a basis for (0 2) tensors, so every such tensor is a sum f_alpha beta omega-tilde^alpha tensor omega-tilde^beta of simple outer products.
concepts.how_introduced: Found by requiring f = f_alpha beta omega-tilde^alpha beta, evaluating on basis vector pairs to force omega-tilde^alpha beta(e_mu, e_nu) = delta^alpha_mu delta^beta_nu, and recognising a product of dual-basis values.

concepts.name: symmetric tensor
concepts.definition: A (0 2) tensor whose value is unchanged when its two arguments are swapped, equivalently with symmetric component matrix; the symmetric part of any h is (h(A,B) + h(B,A))/2, written with round index brackets.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined via argument exchange for all vectors, then specialised to basis vectors; the symmetrisation construction and its bracket notation are introduced because the property is so frequently needed.

concepts.name: antisymmetric tensor
concepts.definition: A (0 2) tensor that changes sign when its arguments are swapped; the antisymmetric part of any h is (h(A,B) - h(B,A))/2, written with square index brackets.
concepts.how_introduced: Paired directly with the symmetric case; Exercise 3.16 shows it vanishes on equal arguments and counts independent components.

concepts.name: symmetric-antisymmetric decomposition
aliases: splitting into symmetric and antisymmetric parts
concepts.definition: Every (0 2) tensor is the sum of its symmetric and antisymmetric parts, and the split is unique.
concepts.how_introduced: Shown by adding and subtracting halves of h_beta alpha; the metric is then noted to be purely symmetric.
concepts.notes: Exercise 3.24(b) asks whether the split makes sense for a (1 1) tensor, a useful probe of index-position understanding.

concepts.name: metric as a map from vectors to one-forms
concepts.definition: The metric with one argument filled by a vector V defines the one-form V-tilde = g(V, _ ), whose value on A is V . A; because g is nondegenerate this correspondence between vectors and one-forms is one-to-one and invertible.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as what the book calls the metric's fundamental role in differential geometry, using the blank-slot notation; components follow in one line, and invertibility is argued from det(eta) = -1.
prerequisites: function versus value of a function
formulas: \tilde V(\vec A)=\mathbf g(\vec V,\vec A)=\vec V\cdot\vec A

concepts.name: index lowering
concepts.definition: Obtaining one-form components from vector components with the metric, V_alpha = eta_alpha beta V^beta; in a Lorentz frame this negates the time component and leaves spatial components unchanged.
concepts.how_introduced: Computed explicitly for alpha = 0 and 1 (Eqs. 3.40-3.41) and summarised as (a,b,c,d) becoming (-a,b,c,d), with a warning that more complicated metrics will give more complicated rules.
prerequisites: metric as a map from vectors to one-forms

concepts.name: inverse metric
concepts.definition: The matrix inverse of eta_alpha beta, with components eta^alpha beta (numerically equal to eta_alpha beta in a Lorentz frame), which maps one-forms to vectors and can be regarded as the (2 0) tensor obtained by raising both indices of g.
concepts.how_introduced: Existence argued from the nonzero determinant of eta; its components given as eta^00 = -1, eta^0i = 0, eta^ij = delta^ij; later used directly to compute one-form magnitudes and reinterpreted as a tensor in §3.8.

concepts.name: vector gradient
concepts.definition: The vector obtained from the gradient one-form by the inverse metric; in a Lorentz frame its components are (-phi_{,t}, phi_{,x}, phi_{,y}, phi_{,z}), and it is orthogonal to every vector tangent to a surface of constant phi.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained as the first application of the inverse map; orthogonality follows because its scalar product with a tangent vector equals the gradient's value on that vector, i.e. the (zero) rate of change of phi within the level surface. Used to argue that a 'vector gradient' defined directly by these sign-flipped components would look unmotivated.
concepts.notes: The book distinguishes the vector by an arrow over d; the markdown export renders both as tilde-d, so the printed page should be consulted.

concepts.name: magnitude of a one-form
concepts.definition: The squared magnitude of a one-form is defined to equal that of its associated vector and can be computed straight from the one-form components with the inverse metric, eta^alpha beta p_alpha p_beta, i.e. minus the square of the time component plus the squares of the spatial ones.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined by borrowing from the associated vector, then the index-raising substitution and the identity eta_alpha beta eta^beta nu = delta collapse the expression so that only the inverse metric appears.

concepts.name: inner product of one-forms
concepts.definition: The symmetric bilinear pairing of one-forms defined by polarisation from magnitudes; in a Lorentz frame it equals eta^alpha beta p_alpha q_beta, a sum with the time-time product negated.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined in direct analogy with the vector case using (p+q)^2, then expressed in components (derivation left to Exercise 3.19).
formulas: \tilde p\cdot\tilde q:=\tfrac12\left[(\tilde p+\tilde q)^2-\tilde p^2-\tilde q^2\right]

concepts.name: timelike, spacelike and null one-forms
concepts.definition: A one-form is timelike, spacelike or null according to whether its magnitude (that of its associated vector) is negative, positive or zero.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated in one sentence once one-form magnitudes are available, inheriting the chapter-2 classification of vectors.

concepts.name: normal vector and unit normal
concepts.definition: A vector is normal to a surface when its associated one-form is a normal one-form (equivalently, its dot product with every tangent vector vanishes); a normal of either kind counts as a unit normal when its squared magnitude is plus or minus one. Null normals cannot be normalised.
concepts.how_introduced: Built on top of the metric-free normal one-form and the metric map, with the remark that the sign of the magnitude cannot be chosen freely because timelike normals have negative magnitude.
prerequisites: metric as a map from vectors to one-forms

concepts.name: causal classification of hypersurfaces
concepts.definition: The book labels a three-dimensional surface timelike, spacelike or null according to the causal type of its normal. Standard usage elsewhere labels a hypersurface by its tangent vectors, so a surface with a timelike normal (such as t = const) is normally called spacelike.
concepts.how_introduced: Given in one sentence at the end of the normals discussion, with self-consistency deferred to Exercise 3.12 and consequences explored in Exercise 3.21.
concepts.notes: This naming is the reverse of the convention in most GR texts; see gaps_and_pitfalls.

concepts.name: outward normal vector
concepts.definition: The vector associated by the metric with an outward normal one-form; its scalar product with any outward-pointing vector is positive, but its own direction can point inward or lie in the surface.
concepts.how_introduced: Described as a set of 'curious properties' previewed from Exercise 3.21: under the book's labelling, it points outward for a spacelike-normal surface, inward for a timelike-normal surface, and is tangent to a null surface; used to argue that the one-form is the more natural normal.
prerequisites: metric as a map from vectors to one-forms
concepts.notes: For the boundary t = 1 of the slab 0 < t < 1, the outward one-form is +d-tilde t but its vector has components (-1, 0, 0, 0), pointing back into the slab.

concepts.name: vectors as linear functions of one-forms
concepts.definition: Any vector V defines a linear map on one-forms, V(p) := p(V); vectors and one-forms are therefore on an equal footing, each the dual of the other.
concepts.how_introduced: Opens §3.7 to 'dethrone' vectors from their privileged role as mere arguments; answered by a 'circular reasoning?' interlude arguing that mutual definition is duality, not circularity, and that physics chooses what to identify with vectors (displacements) or one-forms (gradients).
formulas: \vec V(\tilde p):=\tilde p(\vec V)=p_\alpha V^\alpha:=\langle\tilde p,\vec V\rangle

concepts.name: tensor of type (M N)
concepts.definition: A real-valued function of M one-forms and N vectors that is linear in each argument; its components, obtained by inserting basis one-forms and basis vectors, carry M upper and N lower indices, and a basis is given by outer products of M basis vectors and N basis one-forms.
concepts.how_introduced: Reached in two steps: (M 0) tensors as multilinear functions of one-forms (with V tensor W as example), then the full mixed case exemplified by a (1 1) tensor R(p; A).
prerequisites: vectors as linear functions of one-forms
concepts.notes: Exercise 3.23 asks the reader to prove these tensors form a vector space with the outer-product basis.

concepts.name: transformation law of tensor components
concepts.definition: Each upper index of a tensor's components transforms with Lambda^alpha-bar_mu and each lower index with Lambda^nu_beta-bar, one factor per index, placed as the summation convention requires.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived for a (1 1) tensor by substituting the transformed basis one-forms and vectors into its arguments and using multilinearity (Eq. 3.55); for (0 2) tensors the matrix form f-bar = Lambda^T f Lambda is left to Exercise 3.32.

concepts.name: index raising and lowering
concepts.definition: Using the metric to convert a vector slot of a tensor into a one-form slot (lowering an index) or the inverse metric to do the reverse (raising), changing the tensor's type while keeping its name; in SR moving a time index flips the sign of the component and moving a spatial index does not.
concepts.how_introduced: Generalises the vector-to-one-form map to every slot of an arbitrary tensor, with a (2 1) example showing that lowering different indices yields inequivalent tensors, and the simple SR sign rule.
prerequisites: metric as a map from vectors to one-forms
concepts.notes: Index order matters: horizontal spacing of upper and lower indices records which slot moved.

concepts.name: mixed components of the metric
concepts.definition: Raising one index of the metric gives the Kronecker delta, eta^alpha_beta = eta^alpha mu eta_mu beta = delta^alpha_beta; raising the other index gives back eta^alpha beta, so the inverse metric is the metric with both indices up.
concepts.how_introduced: Computed as the matrix product of mutual inverses, prompting the observation that for g the upper-index components coincide with the inverse matrix of the lower-index components.
concepts.notes: The book adds that g is the only tensor with this property, which is looser than it sounds (see gaps).

concepts.name: metric as added structure
concepts.definition: A bare vector space and its dual carry no scalar product; choosing a nondegenerate symmetric (0 2) tensor to identify vectors with one-forms is extra structure, and whichever tensor plays that role is by definition the metric. Special relativity is the choice of components eta_alpha beta.
concepts.how_introduced: A two-part discussion at the end of §3.8: first why any identification is needed (only if scalar products matter), then why the metric (any tensor doing the job would be called the metric), closing with the pointer that other metric components lead to other geometries, including curved GR spacetime.
prerequisites: metric as a map from vectors to one-forms

concepts.name: Riemannian and pseudo-Riemannian metrics
concepts.definition: A Riemannian metric gives every nonzero vector a positive squared magnitude; a pseudo-Riemannian one, like Minkowski's, allows negative and zero values.
concepts.how_introduced: Named briefly while discussing the metric as structure; the book also mentions antisymmetric 'metrics' on two-dimensional spinor space as out of scope.

concepts.name: nonmetric vector algebra
concepts.definition: A setting with vectors, one-forms and tensors but no preferred identification between vectors and one-forms, so vectors have no scalar product; classical and quantum phase space are cited as places where a metric is not important.
concepts.how_introduced: Hypothetical scenario used to separate what the tensor algebra provides from what the metric adds.

concepts.name: spinor space
concepts.definition: A two-dimensional complex vector space equipped with an antisymmetric bilinear form that plays the role of a metric; fundamental in physics but beyond this book.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned only as an example that a 'metric' need not be symmetric.

concepts.name: gradient of a tensor field
aliases: covariant derivative in a Lorentz frame
concepts.definition: For a tensor field T of type (M N), the (M N+1) tensor nabla T whose components in a Lorentz frame are the partial derivatives of T's components, e.g. T^alpha_{beta,gamma} for a (1 1) field; differentiation adds one covariant slot.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived by differentiating a (1 1) field along a world line, noting the result is a tensor for every tangent U, and removing U to leave a tensor with one more vector slot; justified via the blank-slot argument list nabla T( , U, ).
prerequisites: constant basis in a Lorentz frame
concepts.notes: Called nabla T rather than d-tilde T because d-tilde on tensors is reserved by mathematicians for a different operation (the exterior derivative). Exercise 3.29 proves the Leibniz rule.

concepts.name: directional derivative of a tensor along a vector
concepts.definition: The rate of change of a tensor field along a curve with tangent U, nabla_U T, obtained by filling the derivative slot of nabla T with U; its components are T^alpha_{beta,gamma} U^gamma.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined as the limit of differences of tensors at neighbouring points on a world line (Eq. 3.62), computed with the chain rule, and packaged in new notation (Eqs. 3.67-3.68).
prerequisites: directional derivative of a scalar along a world line

concepts.name: constant basis in a Lorentz frame
concepts.definition: In an inertial (Lorentz) frame the basis vectors and basis one-forms are the same at every event, so derivatives of tensor fields act only on components; this fails for curvilinear coordinates and in curved spacetime.
concepts.how_introduced: Used silently in the step from Eq. 3.62 to 3.63 and then highlighted as the chapter's final sentence: dropping it will be the entry point into GR.

concepts.name: Einstein summation convention
concepts.definition: A repeated index appearing once up and once down is summed over 0-3; distinct summations must use distinct dummy index names.
concepts.how_introduced: Revisited throughout with repeated parenthetical reminders to use different dummy indices for independent sums; Exercise 3.1 contrasts M_alpha beta A^alpha B^beta with the (wrong) single sum over M_alpha alpha A^alpha B^alpha.

concepts.name: Lorentz transformation matrix
concepts.definition: The constant matrix relating coordinates, components and basis vectors of two Lorentz frames; vector components use Lambda^alpha-bar_beta and one-form components and basis vectors use its inverse Lambda^beta_alpha-bar.
concepts.how_introduced: Revisited from chapters 1-2 to derive every transformation law, and identified with coordinate partial derivatives, dx^beta/dx^alpha-bar = Lambda^beta_alpha-bar, because the transformation is linear with constant coefficients.

concepts.name: Lorentz transformation as metric-preserving map
aliases: general definition of a Lorentz transformation
concepts.definition: A Lorentz transformation is any linear change of basis whose matrix leaves the metric components unchanged: eta_alpha-bar beta-bar = Lambda^mu_alpha-bar Lambda^nu_beta-bar eta_mu nu, or in matrix form eta = Lambda^T eta Lambda.
concepts.how_introduced: Proposed in Exercise 3.32 as a more general definition, justified because every Lorentz frame must see components eta; the reader checks that the x-boost satisfies it and that products of such matrices do too.

concepts.name: Lorentz group
concepts.definition: The group of all matrices preserving the Minkowski metric under congruence, with matrix multiplication as the group operation; its elements have determinant +1 or -1, the +1 elements form a subgroup, and the rotation group O(3) sits inside it.
concepts.how_introduced: Named in Exercise 3.33 after Exercise 3.32(c) shows closure under multiplication; the exercise works through identity, inverses, determinants and subgroups.

concepts.name: orthogonal matrix
concepts.definition: A matrix equal to the transpose of its inverse; such matrices are exactly those preserving the Euclidean metric delta_ij, and for them vector and one-form components transform identically.
concepts.how_introduced: Exercise 3.20 uses it to explain why elementary Cartesian vector analysis never needs to distinguish vectors from one-forms.

concepts.name: projection tensor
aliases: P_mu nu = eta_mu nu + U_mu U_nu
concepts.definition: For a unit timelike vector U, the tensor P with components eta_mu nu + U_mu U_nu, which projects any vector onto the subspace orthogonal to U, leaves already-orthogonal vectors unchanged, and acts as the metric on that subspace.
concepts.how_introduced: Exercise 3.31, including the generalisation to any non-null vector q (with q_mu q_nu divided by q^alpha q_alpha) and the question of why null vectors fail.

concepts.name: null basis
concepts.definition: A basis containing null vectors, such as e_u = (e_t - e_x)/2 and e_v = (e_t + e_x)/2 tied to coordinates u = t - x and v = t + x; its vectors are null and mutually non-orthogonal, so the metric components are off-diagonal.
concepts.how_introduced: Exercise 3.34, which asks for the basis, metric components and the relevant one-forms in terms of d-tilde t and d-tilde x.

key_equations.name: Scalar product in components
key_equations.meaning: The dot product of two four-vectors is a double sum of their components weighted by the metric components; this is the seed from which the tensor concept grows.
key_equations.symbols: A^alpha, B^beta: vector components in frame O; eta_alpha beta = diag(-1,1,1,1).

key_equations.name: Linearity of the dot product in the first argument
key_equations.latex: (\alpha\vec A)\cdot\vec B=\alpha(\vec A\cdot\vec B),\qquad(\vec A+\vec B)\cdot\vec C=\vec A\cdot\vec C+\vec B\cdot\vec C
key_equations.meaning: Scaling or splitting the first argument scales or splits the value; the same holds in the second slot. This is the linearity demanded of a tensor.
key_equations.symbols: alpha: real number; A, B, C: vectors.

key_equations.name: Metric tensor defined
key_equations.meaning: Names the dot-product rule as a function g of two vectors, so the metric becomes an object in its own right.
key_equations.symbols: g: metric tensor.

key_equations.name: Bilinearity of g
key_equations.latex: \mathbf g(\alpha\vec A+\beta\vec B,\vec C)=\alpha\,\mathbf g(\vec A,\vec C)+\beta\,\mathbf g(\vec B,\vec C)
key_equations.meaning: Compact statement of linearity in the first slot (and similarly the second).
key_equations.symbols: alpha, beta: real numbers.

key_equations.name: Components of the metric
key_equations.meaning: Feeding basis vectors to g yields its components; in a Lorentz frame these are the Minkowski values.
key_equations.symbols: e_alpha: basis vectors of frame O.

key_equations.label: (3.6a,b)
key_equations.name: Vector-space operations on one-forms
key_equations.latex: \tilde s=\tilde p+\tilde q,\ \tilde r=\alpha\tilde p;\qquad \tilde s(\vec A)=\tilde p(\vec A)+\tilde q(\vec A),\ \tilde r(\vec A)=\alpha\,\tilde p(\vec A)
key_equations.meaning: Sums and multiples of one-forms are defined by their values on vectors, making the one-forms a vector space (the dual space).
key_equations.symbols: p, q: one-forms; alpha: real number.

key_equations.name: Components of a one-form
key_equations.meaning: A one-form's components are its values on the basis vectors; lower index signals one-form.
key_equations.symbols: p_alpha: components of p-tilde.

key_equations.name: Contraction of a one-form with a vector
key_equations.latex: \tilde p(\vec A)=\tilde p(A^\alpha\vec e_\alpha)=A^\alpha\tilde p(\vec e_\alpha)=A^\alpha p_\alpha
key_equations.meaning: By linearity the value of a one-form on a vector is the all-plus-sign sum of products of components, needing no metric.

key_equations.name: Transformation of one-form components
key_equations.meaning: One-form components change with the same matrix as basis vectors (e_beta-bar = Lambda^alpha_beta-bar e_alpha), i.e. inversely to vector components.
key_equations.symbols: Bars mark the new frame; Lambda^alpha_beta-bar: inverse of the matrix Lambda^alpha-bar_beta used for vector components.

key_equations.label: (3.10a-d)
key_equations.name: Frame invariance of contraction
key_equations.meaning: Because vector and one-form components transform with mutually inverse matrices, their contraction is the same in every frame.
key_equations.symbols: The export drops the bars; the printed page (pdf 77) has barred indices on the left side and on the Lambdas.

key_equations.name: Expansion in the dual basis
key_equations.meaning: A one-form is the component-weighted sum of four basis one-forms.
key_equations.symbols: omega-tilde^alpha: basis one-forms.

key_equations.name: Dual basis condition
key_equations.meaning: The basis one-forms are defined by giving 1 on their partner basis vector and 0 on the others, which makes Eq. 3.11 reproduce Eq. 3.8.

key_equations.name: Components of the dual basis
key_equations.meaning: Each dual basis one-form has a single unit component in its own frame.

key_equations.name: Transformation of basis one-forms
key_equations.meaning: Basis one-forms transform like vector components, opposite to one-form components; proof is Exercise 3.7.

key_equations.name: Rate of change of a scalar along a world line
key_equations.meaning: The chain rule expresses the change of phi seen along a world line as a linear function of the four-velocity, which is exactly what a one-form does.
key_equations.symbols: phi: scalar field; tau: proper time; U: four-velocity.

key_equations.name: Gradient one-form components
key_equations.latex: \tilde d\phi\to_{\mathcal O}\left(\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial t},\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial x},\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial y},\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial z}\right)
key_equations.meaning: The gradient of a scalar is the one-form whose components are the partial derivatives.

key_equations.name: Required transformation of gradient components
key_equations.meaning: What the one-form law demands of the gradient.

key_equations.name: Chain-rule transformation of partial derivatives
key_equations.meaning: How partial derivatives actually change under a change of coordinates.

key_equations.name: Coordinate derivative equals the inverse Lorentz matrix
key_equations.meaning: Since old coordinates are constant linear combinations of new ones, the Jacobian is the transformation matrix, reconciling Eqs. 3.16 and 3.17; the book calls this identity fundamental.
key_equations.symbols: Follows from x^beta = Lambda^beta_alpha-bar x^alpha-bar with constant coefficients.

key_equations.name: Comma notation
key_equations.meaning: Shorthand for partial derivatives, with the index lowered to reflect one-form behaviour.

key_equations.name: Derivatives of coordinates
key_equations.meaning: Each coordinate changes only along its own direction, at unit rate.

key_equations.name: Basis one-forms are coordinate gradients
key_equations.meaning: Comparing the previous identity with Eq. 3.12 identifies each dual basis one-form with the gradient of a coordinate.
key_equations.symbols: The book writes ':=' but the relation is derived, not a definition.

key_equations.name: Gradient in the coordinate basis
key_equations.meaning: Expansion of any gradient on the basis d-tilde x^alpha; resembles the infinitesimal differential but is a tensor.

key_equations.name: Components of a (0 2) tensor
key_equations.meaning: Sixteen numbers obtained by feeding pairs of basis vectors.

key_equations.name: Value of a (0 2) tensor
key_equations.meaning: Bilinearity reconstructs the value on any vectors from the components.

key_equations.name: Proposed basis expansion
key_equations.meaning: Ansatz for a basis of (0 2) tensors.

key_equations.name: Condition on the (0 2) basis
key_equations.meaning: Required values of the basis tensors on basis vector pairs (reasoning is Exercise 3.15).

key_equations.name: (0 2) basis as outer products
key_equations.meaning: The required values are products of dual-basis values, so the basis consists of outer products.

key_equations.name: Expansion of a (0 2) tensor
key_equations.meaning: Every (0 2) tensor is a sum of simple outer products.

key_equations.name: Symmetric tensor
key_equations.latex: \mathbf f(\vec A,\vec B)=\mathbf f(\vec B,\vec A)\ \ \forall\vec A,\vec B\quad\Rightarrow\quad f_{\alpha\beta}=f_{\beta\alpha}
key_equations.meaning: Symmetry under argument exchange implies a symmetric component matrix.

key_equations.name: Symmetric part of a tensor
key_equations.latex: \mathbf h_{(s)}(\vec A,\vec B)=\tfrac12\mathbf h(\vec A,\vec B)+\tfrac12\mathbf h(\vec B,\vec A),\qquad h_{(s)\alpha\beta}=\tfrac12(h_{\alpha\beta}+h_{\beta\alpha})
key_equations.meaning: Averaging over argument order produces a symmetric tensor from any (0 2) tensor.

key_equations.name: Symmetrisation brackets
key_equations.meaning: Round brackets on indices denote the symmetric part.

key_equations.name: Antisymmetric tensor
key_equations.latex: \mathbf f(\vec A,\vec B)=-\mathbf f(\vec B,\vec A)\ \ \forall\vec A,\vec B\quad\Rightarrow\quad f_{\alpha\beta}=-f_{\beta\alpha}
key_equations.meaning: Sign change under argument exchange; components form an antisymmetric matrix.

key_equations.name: Antisymmetrisation brackets
key_equations.meaning: Square brackets denote the antisymmetric part (from h_(A)(A,B) = h(A,B)/2 - h(B,A)/2).

key_equations.name: Symmetric-antisymmetric split
key_equations.meaning: Any (0 2) tensor decomposes uniquely into symmetric plus antisymmetric parts.

key_equations.name: Symmetry of the metric
key_equations.latex: \mathbf g(\vec A,\vec B)=\mathbf g(\vec B,\vec A)
key_equations.meaning: The metric is a symmetric tensor.
key_equations.symbols: The book says this follows from Eq. 3.26; it really follows from the symmetry of the dot product or of eta_alpha beta.

key_equations.name: Metric with one slot filled
key_equations.meaning: A vector plugged into one slot of g leaves a linear function of the remaining vector: a one-form.
key_equations.symbols: Blank = slot awaiting a vector.

key_equations.name: Associated one-form
key_equations.latex: \tilde V(\vec A):=\mathbf g(\vec V,\vec A)=\vec V\cdot\vec A
key_equations.meaning: The one-form paired with V gives, on any A, the dot product of V and A.

key_equations.name: Index lowering
key_equations.meaning: The associated one-form's components are the metric contracted with the vector components; index position alone distinguishes them.

key_equations.name: Explicit lowered components
key_equations.meaning: Only the time component changes sign when an index is lowered in a Lorentz frame.

key_equations.name: Sign-flip rule
key_equations.meaning: Mnemonic summary of lowering in Minkowski components.

key_equations.name: Index raising with the inverse metric
key_equations.meaning: The inverse matrix of eta maps one-form components back to vector components, making the correspondence one-to-one.

figures.label: Figure 3.1
figures.caption_paraphrase: Three panels: (a) a one-form drawn as a family of surfaces, the counterpart to an arrow for a vector; (b) its value on a vector is the count of surfaces the arrow pierces; (c) a smaller one-form, with wider spacing, gives a smaller count on the same vector. (Full caption recovered from the rendered page; the export kept only the label.)
figures.visual_description: Three line drawings side by side, labelled (a), (b) and (c). Every line family runs from upper left down to lower right. Panel (a) has five evenly spaced parallel lines and no arrow. Panel (b) repeats the same closely spaced five-line family and adds an arrow that starts low on the left near the first line and rises toward the upper right, crossing roughly three of the lines. Panel (c) has only three lines at about twice the spacing, and an arrow of the same length and direction spans only about two gaps.
figures.what_it_teaches: A one-form is not an arrow but a slicing of space; evaluating it on a vector is counting slices crossed, so denser slicing means a bigger one-form.
concepts: picture of a one-form as stacked surfaces

redesign.idea: Sheet-counter: a 2D canvas with a draggable arrow and a family of parallel lines whose orientation and spacing the learner controls; a live counter shows the (fractional) number of lines crossed next to the component formula p_alpha A^alpha.
redesign.interaction: Drag the arrow tip; rotate the line family and slide its spacing (or directly edit p_x, p_y); toggle to 3D where the lines become planes; highlight that reversing the arrow gives a negative count and that an arrow lying along the lines gives zero.

figures.label: Figure 3.2
figures.caption_paraphrase: A world line labelled by proper time, along which a scalar field phi(t, x, y, z) takes the values phi(tau).
figures.visual_description: A spacetime diagram with vertical t axis and horizontal x axis. A smooth curved world line rises steeply from below the x axis toward the upper right, marked with dots labelled tau = 0 (on the x axis), tau = 1 and tau = 2. At tau = 1 a straight tangent arrow labelled U leaves the curve upward toward the tau = 2 level, and the text phi(tau) = phi[t(tau), x(tau), y(tau), z(tau)] sits beside that point.
figures.what_it_teaches: The rate of change of a field experienced by a moving observer depends linearly on the observer's four-velocity, motivating the gradient as a one-form.
concepts: directional derivative of a scalar along a world line

redesign.idea: Observer in a field: a t-x diagram shaded by a scalar field (e.g. temperature varying in space and time) with a draggable world line; a strip chart shows phi(tau) along it and the value of d phi/d tau at a chosen event, decomposed into phi_{,t} U^t + phi_{,x} U^x.
redesign.interaction: Drag control points to reshape the world line (clamped to be timelike); pick an event with a slider in tau; change the field from a menu; the tangent U, the level lines of phi through the event and the contraction bar chart update together.

figures.label: Figure 3.3
figures.caption_paraphrase: Part of a topographic map with local contours of equal height, illustrating the gradient one-form: the height change along an arrowed path equals the number of contours it crosses.
figures.visual_description: Part of a hillside map drawn with smooth contour lines tagged 10, 20, 30 and 40 at the left edge. The 40 contour is a narrow tongue closing on itself about halfway across. The outer contours run from the left across the map and turn back near the right edge, so the lines crowd together near the upper-left label A and spread apart near the lower-right label B. Circled arrow 1 points straight up from the 10 contour, past the 20 contour, and stops short of 30. Arrows 2 and 3 both start at one point on the right: arrow 2 runs left to the tip of the 30 contour, and arrow 3 runs up and to the left into ground only slightly higher than where it began.
figures.what_it_teaches: The gradient of height is largest where contours are densest; the change in height along a displacement is the gradient evaluated on the displacement, obtained by counting contours without needing distances or angles.
concepts: picture of a one-form as stacked surfaces

redesign.idea: Hiking with a contour map: a procedurally generated terrain shown both as a 3D surface and as a 2D contour map; the learner lays down displacement arrows and the app counts contours crossed and compares with h_{,x} Delta x + h_{,y} Delta y, then zooms in until the contours become straight parallel lines (the one-form at a point).
redesign.interaction: Click-drag arrows on the map; adjust contour interval; toggle a 'zoom to a point' mode that shows the local linear one-form; toggle a metric overlay that draws the steepest-ascent arrow and shows how it changes if the map's horizontal scale is stretched in one direction while the contour counts stay fixed.

figures.label: Figure 3.4
figures.caption_paraphrase: A one-form's surfaces crossed by a vector; the value of the one-form on the vector is 2.5.
figures.visual_description: Five parallel straight lines running from upper left down to lower right, with the one-form symbol omega-tilde written near the bottom right. A roughly horizontal arrow labelled V starts on the leftmost line and ends midway between the third and fourth lines, spanning two and a half gaps.
figures.what_it_teaches: The value of a one-form on a vector can be fractional and is read off as the number of surface spacings the vector spans; at a point the surfaces are straight and parallel.
concepts: picture of a one-form as stacked surfaces

redesign.idea: Fractional counter: a quick quiz widget showing random one-form stacks and arrows; the learner estimates the value, then the app overlays the exact count and the component arithmetic.
redesign.interaction: Type an estimate, reveal answer; slider to change arrow length and see the count change linearly; switch sign by reversing arrow.

figures.label: Figure 3.5
figures.caption_paraphrase: Isotherms (curves of equal temperature) on an unevenly heated plate, used in Exercise 3.9 to estimate gradient components at two marked points.
figures.visual_description: A rectangle with x axis from 0 to 4 and y axis from 0 to 2. A hot spot near (1.1, 1.1) is surrounded by nested closed isotherms labelled 30, 20 and 10, with point P marked just to the right of the 30 loop between the 30 and 20 curves. A second smaller hot spot near (3.7, 0.6) has closed isotherms labelled 20 and 10. Isotherms labelled 0 run through the upper-right corner and across the lower middle, and point Q lies near (3, 1.45) in the region between the 0 curves.
